items.why: Distinguishes the five men who enter and take the objects from the priest and soldiers who remain at the gate.
Requires tracking that the five men take the same items before the priest later takes them along.
Resolves “our king” to the speaking trees rather than to the gods and humans mentioned earlier.
Links prosperity specifically to the land lacking nothing, not to the comparison with Sidonian life.
Separates the explicit inheritance-based cause from the nearby statement that Israel lacked a king.
Connects Jotham’s relocation to fear of Abimelek rather than to the later-mentioned Shechemites.
Distinguishes the relatives receiving Abimelek’s instruction from the citizens who are to receive the message.
Separates the Levite’s purpose in leaving from Micah’s house, which he reaches only incidentally en route.
Tests sequence between the mutual-joy wish and the following fire curse, though calling the wish a request is imprecise.
Requires resolving “for him” to the young Levite, but the question’s phrase “does something” is vague.
Distinguishes the report that triggers the ambush from Abimelek’s later sight of people leaving the city.
Contrasts the mother’s stated agent, her son, with the silversmith who actually makes the image later.
Requires resolving “him” and “he” to Abimelek rather than misassigning the death to the servant.
Identifies the fire as the fatal cause rather than the occupants’ earlier movement into the stronghold.
Separates the priesthood’s duration until captivity from the idol’s duration while God’s house was at Shiloh.
Uses the immediate shouting-turning relation rather than the earlier fact that Micah’s men overtook them.
Links the fig tree’s refusal to surrendering its fruit, not to the trees’ subsequent appeal to the vine.
Distinguishes Abimelek’s specific purpose at the doorway—setting the tower on fire—from his broader attack.
Resolves the object of “take it over” as the land rather than the people living there.
Selects Micah’s explicit reason—having the Levite as priest—over the Levite’s place of origin.
Requires ordering the hill country after the Kiriath Jearim camp and immediately before Micah’s house.
Resolves “him” through the fairness question and “my father” reference to Jerub-Baal, not Abimelek.
Distinguishes Zebul as the secret sender from Gaal, whose actions motivate the message.
Separates the priest they address from God, whom the priest is asked to consult.
The curse follows in the discourse, but it may describe God’s punishment rather than a clearly subsequent event.
Tracks Zebul’s reply to Gaal’s first claim and contrasts shadows with the people Gaal reports seeing.
Keeps Jotham’s stated purpose for listening separate from the king-anointing event inside his parable.
Links the olive tree’s refusal to giving up its oil rather than to the trees’ later turn to the fig tree.
Uses Micah’s second-person reference to identify his mother as the one who uttered the curse.
Distinguishes the festival meal during the curse from the earlier grape gathering and treading.
Selects distance and lack of alliances as the reason no rescuer comes, not the attack itself.
